doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Students, Nicholas Payton and the need for mature players
summary: Students want fame but are weak on chord changes; he praises Nicholas Payton and Doc Cheatham and says swing does not mean fast.

venues.name: New Orleans Center for Creative Arts

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: So the music and the marketing are two completely different camps.

They’re just two different things. And like I say, a lot of people will argue with me, but a lot of the students that I teach, like I said earlier, their main goal is to be famous. Well man, “I’m trying to get this contract.” What are you going to do when you get the contract, son, you know? I’m sitting right here in the classroom with you and you know, when it comes to, you know, just some modal type of thing where they can do all kinds of jazzy, funny stuff on the instrument, they do quite well. But when it comes to playing inside of the chords, that’s where they have the weakness. And I don’t know, you have to know the rules before you can break the rules. And this is, I don’t know, I think we’re going to have to record more people with more experience. This is the way these younger guys are going to learn, you know? But I mean a lot of those young guys have great energy. I have a kid right now who’s been around me ever since he was about six years old. His name is Nicholas Payton, you know of him?

He is a killer. But he grew up, he played in those New Orleans brass bands, and he, you know, he used to come around me a lot and then he went to a little school in New Orleans called NOCA, the New Orleans Center for the Creative Arts. And that brought him out. He learned his theory and this guy plays piano, he’s a great drummer, plays bass, his dad is a bass player. He plays bass like unbelievable. And he’s blowing the bell off of the trumpet. So there are exceptions to these things that I’m saying. But we’re going to have to start recording some more mature people so the guys will get an idea of what a mature player plays like. You know how Dan was saying first he was trying to do all kinds of ripping and running and stuff like that? And eventually he learned, hey man, slow down, take your time. And this is what the younger players are going to learn from the more mature players. And I mean like when you hear Doc Cheatham man, you don’t want to hear any more trumpet than that. He’s swinging, he’s just playing, I mean there is just so much there. And he’s played like that for fifty, sixty, seventy years now. I mean Doc is 90, maybe 91 now. So I mean you know it’s so important. Swing is so important. And swing does not mean fast. This is another misinterpretation we got going here. Swing does not mean fast.
